cells.tense: Right now the patterns arrive stripped of their content, and there is room while you carry what you carry.
cells.ask: Pick the one pattern you've recognised this week and say it out loud to someone who can use it. Just the shape of it, not the story around it.
cells.core:
Something is holding you up while you read the shape of it. Most people who can see how a thing works lose the floor under them doing it — they float off into the idea and leave the weight behind. You don't. You can name the mechanism of the thing you're carrying and still be carrying it.

That combination is rarer than it sounds and you may not have noticed it as yours. The clear seeing, the shoulders. The load isn't smaller because you understand it — understanding it doesn't lift anything — but the shoulders have more slack in them now, and seeing feeds that. There's a pull toward something brighter you can let deepen from the same center. What that asks of you is small: the next time a pattern comes clear, hand it to one person who can use it, and notice that it didn't get heavier. Then decide whether you want to do that again.
cells.sheetLine: You hold the weight and read its shape at once.
cells.verb: seeing the shape of the thing stripped of its content
cells.place: under a load that has to keep being held

cells.tense: There is a version of this ahead where you'll finally have it figured out, and you're bracing for it now.
cells.ask: Set a clock for twenty minutes. Read one pattern, say what it means, stop when the clock does, finished or not.
cells.core:
There is something ahead you're watching that hasn't arrived. The machine starts up and you're already there, scanning for the flaw you'll find the next time you look. Patterns run one into another and there's no end to how many you can draw. The shoulders are still taking the weight.

The part that costs you is this: you look, and look, and look. The analysis does not run out on its own. What does run out is the night, the person you were talking to, the chance to have said the one true thing in front of you. There is a smaller, more structural move available. Put a limit on the reading that isn't a feeling — a clock, a page, one more question and then you stop — and let what's underneath take its own weight for a while. That's not defeat. That's what a frame is for.

cells.tense: You take what arrives at face value, and that habit has outlasted whatever made it reasonable.
cells.ask: Take one story you love and tell someone what it's actually about. Stay in the telling after it gets uncomfortable.
cells.core:
You take things as they come and don't ask them for a second layer — the load gets carried, the day gets done, and the pattern behind it gets left alone. At some point that was the reasonable thing to do, and the shape it gave hasn't worn off.

What you don't have right now isn't the ability to think deeply. It's that the depth has nowhere to stand while the weight's on your back, so you don't let the weight get read at all. There's a way back that doesn't start with pushing harder or feeling more. It starts with other people's meaning — a story, a practice, a way of telling things that someone else made and you can carry for a while. Let one of those be yours. Seeing gets easier when it doesn't have to be invented alone.

cells.tense: You read people's mechanisms off them all day and call it reading the room, when it's you picking what gets repeated.
cells.ask: Pick one rule you've obeyed today — written or not — and write down who wrote it, with a name.
cells.core:
You already notice how things fit together. People come to you with a problem and you have the shape of it before they've finished. Standing in the middle of it, carrying it, you're reading the structure underneath without saying so, and then treating the structure as just how things are.

That reading is doing work when you decide what's worth saying and what isn't, and the page under it is blank — that's the part that isn't there. Somebody set this. Maybe you did. Somebody has been in charge of what you carry and what you let go, and you haven't looked at that in a while. The smaller move on offer: pick one thing you're carrying, find the shape of it, and notice whose shape it actually is. Carrying gets cleaner when you can see the hands.
